name: Docker Desktop Pro and Team
summary: Docker Desktop is Docker's desktop application for Mac, Windows and Linux, versioned 4.x independently of Docker Engine. Docker scopes supported versions by subscription edition: the Pro and Team editions are supported on the latest version only, so a release's support ends when a newer version is published. The record is edition-scoped because one release-level end-of-life cannot state two different plan rules.

Versions older than the latest release (except Docker Business)

notes: Tier: researched, with per-release derived end-of-life dates (AGENTS.md rule 8b). Docker Desktop is the desktop application, versioned 4.x independently of Docker Engine; data/products/docker-engine.json is a separate product, is neither touched nor referenced as a lifecycle parent. No deterministic source covers Desktop: https://endoflife.date/api/all.json lists 477 products (checked 2026-09-23) with no docker-desktop slug, and data/products/ holds no docker-desktop record, so this contribution neither overwrites nor shadows a pipeline. GA dates are the release dates the official release-notes page publishes for each 4.x release, quoted verbatim above (one quote per release). Every eol here is DERIVED, not vendor-stated: Docker publishes no per-version Desktop end date, but its support page states the edition's supported-versions rule and the release notes date every release, so the ending release is named and its published date is the derived deadline under milestone_provenance with method release-trigger. Derived dates are presented as derived and are excluded from the exact-day Atom/RSS/iCalendar feeds and the OpenEoX export with machine-readable disclosure. eossec stays null everywhere: 'fixes applied to latest version only' says which version receives fixes, not a separate dated security-support end, and mapping it to eossec would turn a support-scope statement into a security milestone. eos stays null: Docker publishes no Desktop end-of-sale date. Deliberately NOT used as lifecycle evidence: the release-notes statement that versions older than six months from the latest release are not available for download (a download-availability cutoff, not a support end); the macOS compatibility rule ('current and two previous major macOS releases', a host requirement, not inherited lifecycle); the weekly release cadence; and release activity on older lines. Docker backports fixes to older lines in parallel (4.32.1/4.33.2/4.34.4/4.35.2/4.36.1 all carry the 2025-01-09 date of one vmnetd/socket fix, while 4.37.0 had already shipped on 2024-12-12), so a patch on an older line is not a successor version. 4.37.2 shipped on that same 2025-01-09 date but was the newest version then and is derived normally; the lower-versioned backports were never the latest version and keep no eol. Three release rows carry no unambiguous ISO release date on the page: 4.31.0 and 4.31.1 are undated, and 4.4.2 is dated '22-01-13', which is not an ISO day, so no date is invented for any of them and their rows stay unknown rather than being dropped or padded. Edition rule (verbatim above): 'Docker Pro and Team: Latest version only', with 'Versions older than the latest release (except Docker Business)' excluded. Each release's support therefore ends at the next release that becomes the latest version, and the trigger names that release. A row that was already behind a higher version when it shipped was never 'the latest version' and is published with no eol rather than a date the rule does not produce, as are the parallel maintenance patches on older lines (4.32.1 through 4.36.1). Unknown rows are accounted for, not dropped: 4.92.0: no release with a newer version and a published date past 2026-09-21 exists yet; 4.36.1: a higher version was already published before this release shipped, so this release was never the latest version and the rule names no window for it; 4.35.2: a higher version was already published before this release shipped, so this release was never the latest version and the rule names no window for it; 4.34.4: a higher version was already published before this release shipped, so this release was never the latest version and the rule names no window for it; 4.33.2: a higher version was already published before this release shipped, so this release was never the latest version and the rule names no window for it; 4.32.1: a higher version was already published before this release shipped, so this release was never the latest version and the rule names no window for it; 4.31.1: the release-notes page states no ISO release date for this release (cell: None), so there is no base date; 4.31.0: the release-notes page states no ISO release date for this release (cell: None), so there is no base date; 4.30.0: 4.31.0 carries a newer version than this release, and the page leaves its release date open between the releases either side of it, so the release that ended support cannot be named; 4.4.2: the release-notes page states no ISO release date for this release (cell: '22-01-13'), so there is no base date; 4.3.2: 4.4.2 carries a newer version than this release, and the page leaves its release date open between the releases either side of it, so the release that ended support cannot be named. 139 of 150 releases carry a derived eol and 11 stay unknown. Docker Desktop 4.92.0 is the current latest version, so it has no eol: no newer version has been published.
